jdso8u-d1e149-d1e107.summary: Editorial title (Wadding numbering: 'lateral' questions 3 and 4 of the prologue) for the questions whether theology in itself is a science and whether it is a subalternating or subalternated science.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e123.summary: Scotus poses both questions and answers the first by defining science in the strict Aristotelian sense (Posterior Analytics I) through four conditions: certain cognition, without error or doubt; of a necessary object; caused by an evident cause; applied to the known by syllogistic reasoning. The fourth, discursive causation from cause to conclusion, implies imperfection (an equivocal effect) and potentiality in the receiving intellect. So theology in itself, and in the divine intellect, is a science in the first three respects but not the fourth.
claims: Science in the strict sense requires certainty, a necessary object, evidence from a cause, and syllogistic discourse.
Discursive causation implies imperfection in the science and potentiality in the intellect.
Theology in itself, and in God's intellect, meets the first three conditions but not the fourth.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e187.summary: Raises the doubt whether the blessed have theology as science in the fourth, discursive sense, and argues no from Augustine (De Trinitate XV.16): in heaven our thoughts may no longer move to and fro but we will see our knowledge in a single glance, so the blessed do not reason discursively.
claims: Augustine suggests the blessed see all their knowledge in a single intuition without discursive thought.
If so, the blessed would lack the fourth condition of science.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e226.summary: Argument for the opposite: the quiddity of a subject, in whatever light it is seen, virtually contains the truths it can make known. If the quiddity of a line seen in natural light makes its truths known to us, so does it when seen in the divine essence. Any truth caused in the intellect by something naturally prior is caused by discourse, because discourse requires only an order of nature (the principle known first and causing knowledge of the conclusion), not temporal succession.
claims: A quiddity virtually contains the truths it can make known, in any light in which it is seen.
Discourse requires only a natural order of priority between principle and conclusion, not temporal succession.
So the blessed, who know truths through prior principles, can have discursive knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e272.summary: Scotus concedes that the blessed can truly have theological science with all its conditions. Augustine's text is not decisive: he speaks hesitantly ('fortasse'), and his point is that our word is never equal to God's Word however perfect. Alternatively it can be read as concerning the beatific vision of God's essential attributes only.
claims: The blessed can have theology as science in all four conditions.
Augustine's remark is tentative and concerns the inequality of our word and the divine Word, or only the vision of God's essentials.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e318.summary: A further doubt: theology covers contingent truths as well as necessary ones. All the articles on the Incarnation are contingent, and even the theology of the blessed includes contingent truths about God's relation to creatures. Since by definition there is no science of contingents, theology as a whole does not seem to be a science, with or without discourse.
claims: Theology includes contingent truths, such as those about the Incarnation and about God's relations to creatures.
There is no science of contingents by definition.
So theology as a whole seems not to be a science.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e361.summary: Reply: what perfects a cognition is being evident and certain; necessity is a condition of the object, not of the cognition, since even knowledge of necessary things can itself be contingent and lost through forgetting. A cognition that is certain, evident and of itself perpetual is formally more perfect than a science that merely requires a necessary object. Theological contingents can be known with such certainty and perpetual evidence, since they and their connection are apt to be seen in theology's first object.
claims: Evidence and certainty are what make a cognition perfect; necessity belongs to the object, not the cognition.
Knowledge of necessary truths can itself be contingent and forgotten.
Theological contingent truths can be known with certain, evident and perpetual cognition because they are seen in the first object of theology.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e419.summary: Completes the argument: seeing the terms of a contingent truth and their union necessarily produces evident certainty about it, and since the theological object that reveals such truths is, of itself, perpetual, theological contingents can be known more perfectly than through acquired science of necessary truths.
claims: Seeing the terms of a contingent truth and their union necessarily causes evident certainty of it.
Theological contingents can be known more perfectly than acquired science of necessary truths.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e450.summary: Is such knowledge of contingents science? In the Posterior Analytics sense, which requires a necessary object, no: knowing a contingent as necessary is not knowing it. In the broader sense of Nicomachean Ethics VI, where science is contrasted with opinion and suspicion as a habit by which we determinately say what is true, it can be science.
claims: Knowledge of contingents is not science in the Posterior Analytics sense.
It is science in the broader sense of Ethics VI, as a habit of determinately grasping truth.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e492.summary: Scotus judges that theology in itself is more properly called wisdom: for its necessary truths it has evidence, necessity, certainty and the highest object, and its contingent truths are evident as seen directly in the theological object, not through evidence borrowed from prior truths. So its knowledge of contingents is more like understanding of principles than science of conclusions.
claims: Theology in itself is more properly wisdom than science.
Its contingent truths are evident in themselves in the theological object, not derived from prior truths.
Theological knowledge of contingents resembles understanding of principles rather than demonstrative science.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e533.summary: Turning to the second question, Scotus holds that theology is not subalternated to any science. Although its subject may be contained in some way under the subject of metaphysics, it takes no principles from metaphysics, since no theological attribute can be demonstrated through principles or reasons of being. Nor does it subalternate any other science, since no other science takes its principles from theology; every natural science resolves finally into immediate principles known naturally.
claims: Theology in itself is not subalternated to metaphysics or any science.
No theological attribute can be demonstrated from the notion of being.
Theology subalternates no other science, because natural sciences resolve into naturally known principles.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e576.summary: Objection: resolution of knowledge stops only at the most perfectly knowable thing, known most perfectly. A line is known more perfectly in the Word than by its own motion on the intellect, so conclusions and principles about a line ultimately resolve into the vision of the Word. Theology would then subalternate all other knowledge by giving them evidence.
claims: Resolution of knowledge ends only in what is most perfectly known.
A line is known more perfectly in the Word than by itself.
So all knowledge resolves to the vision of the Word, which would subalternate other sciences.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e619.summary: Reply, using an analogy: a metaphysician who knows the quiddity of a line distinctly knows an immediate principle about it more perfectly than a geometer who knows the line only confusedly, yet the proposition is self-evident to the geometer from his confused concept of the terms and is not proved through the metaphysician's knowledge. This would be clearer still if the line were known through different moving causes, equally distinctly on the side of the object but not equally clearly.
claims: A principle can be self-evident from a confused concept of its terms and also known more perfectly from a distinct concept.
The more perfect knower does not thereby prove the principle for the less perfect knower.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e671.summary: Application: an immediate principle about a line is evident to an intellect moved by the line, and more clearly to one moved by the Word, but the principle known one way does not demonstrate itself known the other way; it is self-evident both ways, only with different clarity. Subalternation requires that knowledge of the higher science's principles cause knowledge of the lower's principles, which does not happen here. This concludes the treatment of theology in itself.
claims: A principle known in the Word and known from the line is self-evident in both cases, differing only in clarity.
Subalternation requires that the higher science's principles cause knowledge of the lower's principles.
So the vision of the Word does not subalternate natural sciences.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e712.summary: Turns to our theology (theology as had by wayfarers): would it be subalternated if such knowledge were given to someone, or has it been given? Some (the Thomist position) say it is subalternated to the science of God and the blessed.
claims: Some hold that our theology is subalternated to the science of God and the blessed.
concepts: science of God and the blessed

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e732.summary: Arguments against that view: (1) its proponents elsewhere say science cannot coexist with faith, yet here say a subalternated science coexists with faith, which is self-contradictory; (2) there can be only one science of God, so none is subalternated; (3) a science depends causally only on its object, subject or light, but the vision of the blessed has no causal role for the wayfarer's intellect.
claims: The subalternation view contradicts its proponents' claim that science and faith cannot coexist.
There is only one science of God, so none can be subalternated to another.
The blessed's vision exercises no causality on the wayfarer's knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e149-d1e770.summary: Further arguments: (4) subalternating and subalternated sciences are not primarily about the same truths, since the lower begins where the higher ends, but our theology can be about the same truths as the blessed's; (5) whoever has a subalternated science can have the subalternating one and vice versa, yet a wayfarer cannot see clearly and a blessed person cannot have faith. Both premisses of the last argument are defended.
claims: Subalternating and subalternated sciences do not primarily concern the same truths.
Our theology can concern the same truths as that of the blessed.
One who has a subalternated science can have the subalternating one, and vice versa, which is impossible between wayfarer and blessed.

jdso8u-d1e149.summary: Ordinatio I, Prologue part 4 (Wadding 'lateral' questions 3-4): whether theology in itself is a science and whether it is subalternating or subalternated. Using the four Aristotelian conditions of science (certainty, necessary object, evident cause, syllogistic discourse), Scotus holds that theology in itself and in God meets all but discursive causation, which implies imperfection, while the blessed can have it with all four, Augustine notwithstanding. Since theology also covers contingent truths, he argues that evidence and certainty, not the necessity of the object, make a cognition perfect: theological contingents seen in the first object are known more perfectly than acquired science. They are science only in the broad sense of Ethics VI, and theology in itself is better called wisdom, its knowledge of contingents being more like understanding of principles. Theology in itself is neither subalternated to metaphysics nor subalternating other sciences: knowing a principle more clearly in the Word does not cause its self-evidence. The question then turns to our theology, setting out arguments against the view that it is subalternated to the science of God and the blessed.
claims: Theology in itself is a science in the first three conditions, though not discursively caused.
The blessed can have theology as science in all four conditions.
Evidence and certainty, not necessity of object, constitute the perfection of cognition.
Theology in itself is more properly wisdom.
Theology in itself is neither subalternated nor subalternating.
Our theology is not, as some claim, subalternated to the science of God and the blessed.
